title: Journey to the Deep
sources: Monterey Bay Aquarium and MBARI (montereybayaquarium.org, mbari.org)

finish.title: Challenger Deep
finish.blurb: You reached the deepest known part of the ocean, about 35,876 feet down in the Mariana Trench. Only a few explorers have ever been this deep. Nice diving!

zones.name: Above the Waves
zones.blurb: Sunny open water and sky, where sea birds soar and dive.

zones.name: The Sunlight Zone
zones.blurb: Bright warm water where almost all ocean life lives, including the coral reefs.

zones.name: The Twilight Zone
zones.blurb: Only a whisper of blue light. Many animals here make their own glow.

zones.name: The Midnight Zone
zones.blurb: No sunlight ever reaches here. It is always pitch black.

zones.name: The Trench
zones.blurb: The deepest cracks in the whole ocean floor.

zones.name: Hydrothermal Vents
zones.blurb: Cracks in the sea floor gush water hotter than an oven, and life crowds around them.

creatures.name: Albatross
creatures.fact: The wandering albatross has the longest wings of any bird alive, wider than a car is long, so it can glide over the ocean for hours without flapping.
facts: The wandering albatross has the longest wings of any bird alive, wider than a car is long, so it can glide over the ocean for hours without flapping.
Albatrosses can even sleep while they fly, catching little naps in the air as they glide over the open sea.
An albatross can spend years out at sea without ever touching land, only coming ashore to raise a chick.
asks: How does it glide for so long?
Where do albatrosses sleep?
creatures.source: National Geographic Kids; NOAA Ocean Service

creatures.name: Pelican
creatures.fact: A pelican scoops up fish in the big stretchy pouch under its beak, like catching them in a net, then tips its head to drain the water out.
facts: A pelican scoops up fish in the big stretchy pouch under its beak, like catching them in a net, then tips its head to drain the water out.
Brown pelicans dive from high in the air and hit the water with a big splash to surprise the fish below.
A pelican's pouch can hold more water than its stomach can, so it always drains the water before swallowing its catch.
asks: Why does a pelican have a pouch?
How deep do pelicans dive?

creatures.name: Sea Turtle
creatures.fact: Sea turtles can hold their breath for hours while they rest, and they cry salty tears to get rid of extra sea salt.
facts: Sea turtles can hold their breath for hours while they rest, and they cry salty tears to get rid of extra sea salt.
Some sea turtles swim across entire oceans and return to the exact beach where they hatched.
Sea turtles have been around for more than 100 million years, since the dinosaurs!
asks: How do turtles find their home beach?
How long do sea turtles live?

creatures.name: Dolphin
creatures.fact: Dolphins talk with clicks and whistles, and each dolphin has its own special name-whistle!
facts: Dolphins talk with clicks and whistles, and each dolphin has its own special name-whistle!
Dolphins sleep with one half of their brain at a time so they can keep swimming and breathing.
Dolphins find fish with sound, sending out clicks and listening for the echoes.

stats.label: Sleeps with
stats.value: Half a brain at a time

asks: How do dolphins use sound to see?
Do dolphins really have names?

creatures.name: Clownfish and Anemone
creatures.fact: A clownfish lives right inside a stinging sea anemone, which would hurt most fish, but a slimy coat keeps the clownfish safe from the sting.
facts: A clownfish lives right inside a stinging sea anemone, which would hurt most fish, but a slimy coat keeps the clownfish safe from the sting.
The clownfish and the anemone help each other: the anemone hides the clownfish, and the clownfish chases away fish that would nibble the anemone.
Every clownfish is born male, and the biggest one in the group can turn into a female. The whole family shares one anemone home.
asks: Why doesn't the anemone sting it?
What is a sea anemone?
creatures.source: NOAA National Ocean Service; Monterey Bay Aquarium

creatures.name: Reef Shark
creatures.fact: Reef sharks patrol the coral reef looking for fish, and they help keep the reef healthy by catching the sick and slow ones.
facts: Reef sharks patrol the coral reef looking for fish, and they help keep the reef healthy by catching the sick and slow ones.
Sharks can smell a tiny drop of blood in the water from far away, and they feel the wiggles of other fish with special sense spots on their skin.
A shark's skeleton is made of bendy cartilage, the same stuff inside your ears and nose, not hard bone like ours.
asks: How do sharks smell so well?
Are reef sharks dangerous to people?

creatures.name: Glowing Jellyfish
creatures.fact: Many deep-sea jellyfish glow in the dark, making light with special chemicals, like living lanterns.
facts: Many deep-sea jellyfish glow in the dark, making light with special chemicals, like living lanterns.
Jellyfish have no brain, no heart, and no bones, and they have drifted the oceans for 500 million years.
Some jellyfish flash bright patterns to startle predators, then slip away into the dark.
asks: How does a jellyfish glow?
Can a jellyfish think without a brain?
creatures.source: Monterey Bay Aquarium; NOAA Ocean Exploration

creatures.name: Hatchetfish
creatures.fact: The hatchetfish has rows of tiny lights on its belly that glow softly, so from below it blends into the faint light and hungry fish cannot see its shadow.
facts: The hatchetfish has rows of tiny lights on its belly that glow softly, so from below it blends into the faint light and hungry fish cannot see its shadow.
Its huge eyes point upward to catch the last bits of sunlight and spot food drifting down from above.
A hatchetfish is thin and shiny like a coin standing on its edge, which is how it got its hatchet shape and name.
asks: Why does it glow on its belly?
How big is a hatchetfish?

creatures.name: Anglerfish
creatures.fact: The anglerfish carries a glowing light above its mouth like a fishing rod. Curious fish swim to the light, and SNAP!
facts: The anglerfish carries a glowing light above its mouth like a fishing rod. Curious fish swim to the light, and SNAP!
An anglerfish's teeth point inward, so anything that swims in cannot swim back out.
The lure's light comes from billions of tiny glowing bacteria that live inside it. The fish and the bacteria help each other!
asks: How does the lure light up?
Why point its teeth inward?

creatures.name: Giant Squid
creatures.fact: The giant squid has the biggest eyes of any animal on Earth, each about the size of a dinner plate.
facts: The giant squid has the biggest eyes of any animal on Earth, each about the size of a dinner plate.
Giant squid can grow longer than a school bus, but are so shy that one was not filmed alive until 2004.
Their arms are covered in suckers ringed with tiny teeth for gripping slippery prey.
asks: Why are its eyes so big?
How long is a giant squid?

creatures.name: Gulper Eel
creatures.fact: The gulper eel has a giant mouth that opens like a balloon, so it can swallow prey much bigger than itself.
facts: The gulper eel has a giant mouth that opens like a balloon, so it can swallow prey much bigger than itself.
Its long thin tail has a glowing pink tip that it can wave like a lure to draw curious animals close in the dark.
Most of the gulper eel is really just its stretchy mouth and belly, made to grab any rare meal that comes along where food is scarce.
asks: How wide can its mouth open?
Why is food so rare down here?
creatures.source: NOAA Ocean Exploration; Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute

creatures.name: Dumbo Octopus
creatures.fact: The dumbo octopus flaps two fins like elephant ears to swim, which is how it got its name.
facts: The dumbo octopus flaps two fins like elephant ears to swim, which is how it got its name.
It lives deeper than almost any other octopus, gliding where the water is near freezing.
It does not squirt ink like other octopuses. Down here, there is almost nobody to hide from!
asks: Why doesn't it need ink?
How deep does it live?

creatures.name: Hadal Snailfish
creatures.fact: The deepest-living fish ever found, seen more than 27,000 feet down, deeper than Mount Everest is tall!
facts: The deepest-living fish ever found, seen more than 27,000 feet down, deeper than Mount Everest is tall!
Snailfish look soft and ghostly with see-through skin, perfect for surviving the crushing pressure.
At these depths the pressure would crush a submarine's windows, but the snailfish wiggles happily along.
asks: How does it survive the pressure?
What does it eat down there?
creatures.source: University of Washington; NOAA Ocean Exploration

creatures.name: Giant Tube Worms
creatures.fact: Giant tube worms live in tall white tubes near hot cracks in the sea floor and can grow taller than a grown-up, with no eyes and no mouth at all.
facts: Giant tube worms live in tall white tubes near hot cracks in the sea floor and can grow taller than a grown-up, with no eyes and no mouth at all.
They never eat food. Tiny bacteria live inside them and make food from the chemicals in the hot water, then share it with the worm.
Their bright red plumes are full of blood that soaks up chemicals from the vent water to feed the bacteria inside.
asks: How do they eat with no mouth?
What comes out of the vents?
creatures.source: NOAA Ocean Exploration; Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution

creatures.name: Yeti Crab
creatures.fact: The yeti crab has fuzzy, hairy arms that look like a tiny snow monster, which is how it got its nickname.
facts: The yeti crab has fuzzy, hairy arms that look like a tiny snow monster, which is how it got its nickname.
It grows gardens of bacteria on its hairy arms, waves them over the warm vent water to help the bacteria grow, then eats them like a farmer eats crops.
Yeti crabs were only discovered in 2005, deep near vents in the cold dark, far from any sunlight.
asks: Why are its arms hairy?
How does it farm its food?

creatures.name: Vent Shrimp
creatures.fact: Thousands of vent shrimp swarm over the hot vents, so many that they pile right on top of each other near the warm water.
facts: Thousands of vent shrimp swarm over the hot vents, so many that they pile right on top of each other near the warm water.
Vent shrimp have no normal eyes. Instead they have a special patch on their back that senses the faint glow of the super hot vents, so they do not cook.
Like their vent neighbors, they live on bacteria that make food from vent chemicals, with no sunlight at all.
asks: How do they see with no eyes?
Why don't they get cooked?
